Paper_name: Socio-cognitive training impacts emotional and perceptual self-salience but not self-other distinction
Summary: This study examined whether a socio-cognitive training (counter-imitation, Santiesteban et al. 2012) specifically enhances self-other distinction, or rather modulates relative self-salience (the attentional priority of self-related information). Across two experiments, participants trained on day 1 to imitate, inhibit imitation, inhibit control stimuli, or (in Experiment 1 only) to be imitated. On day 2 they completed an affective touch (visuo-tactile empathy) task and a shape matching task (Sui et al. 2012). Results showed no significant or consistent impact of training on self-other distinction, but increased emotional and perceptual self-salience following imitation-inhibition training.
Author: Henryk Bukowski, Boryana Todorova, Magdalena Boch, Giorgia Silani, Claus Lamm
Extra_Var: Training group (between-subjects: imitation / imitation-inhibition / control-inhibition / be-imitated in Exp 1; three groups in Exp 2); IRI, cEQ, PANAS (questionnaires)
Conclusion: Imitation-inhibition training did not enhance self-other distinction in empathy, but consistently (across both experiments and both tasks) increased self-salience - the prioritization of self-related over other-related information - although with variable statistical reliability and small effect sizes. The results invite considering self-salience as a complementary explanation for past, present and future findings on self-other distinction, and do not clearly support the cross-domain generality of either mechanism.
